headline: High: shared write-capable agent plus dbt can create unsafe downstream actions and data-handling mismatches; prompt-injection and leakage are lower-confidence due to limited pairwise evidence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP, stdin/stdout, shell, and subprocesses, so it can ingest untrusted content; agent_b (dbt-core) consumes warehouse-facing inputs and can be driven by upstream artifacts. No shared channel is explicitly documented, so this is inferred and uncertainty pushes severity up from low.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards raw model output into an MCP tool or stdin pipeline that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF a shared workspace or message queue is introduced between agent_a and agent_b
mitigations: Disable automatic parsing of agent_a outputs as commands
Add a strict allowlist for MCP tool arguments
Insert a human review step before dbt execution
Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and performance metrics, while agent_b touches data warehouse data. Both have allowlisted network egress, so if they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive material can flow from A into B or vice versa. The exact bridge is undocumented, so medium is the higher safe choice.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a filesystem, repo checkout, or credential store
IF either agent uploads file contents or query artifacts to its backend by default
mitigations: Keep separate service accounts and credentials
Mount separate workspaces for each agent
Redact prompts and repository metadata before handoff
Review outbound allowlists for both agents
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b is a dbt-core workflow that commonly operates on shared warehouse resources. Overlap on mutable resources is plausible, but the profiles do not prove a shared directory or locking failure, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository or working directory
IF dbt runs against artifacts that agent_a mutates concurrently
mitigations: Run the agents in separate checkouts
Serialize writes to git and build artifacts
Use file locks around shared outputs
Limit agent_a to read-only access during dbt runs
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate or transform task artifacts, and agent_b can act on warehouse-facing inputs; if B treats A's output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into incorrect models or production data changes. Because no verification or provenance controls are documented, the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-produced SQL, manifests, or prompts without validation
IF agent_a is allowed to alter dbt inputs that feed production runs
mitigations: Require schema validation on all handoffs
Add a diff review before dbt execution
Block direct promotion from agent_a output to production
Log and compare expected vs actual warehouse changes
requires-engineering: add signed artifacts and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles repository metadata and task prompts, while agent_b handles data warehouse data; the profiles do not show a residency or regulated-data mismatch. Because no compliance controls are documented for either agent, only a small documented-gap risk remains, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared warehouse path without a DPA or retention policy
IF agent_a is used to process data subject to residency rules
mitigations: Classify data before handoff
Confirm retention settings for warehouse outputs
Avoid placing regulated data in agent_a prompts
Document the data-processing boundary
requires-engineering: add residency and retention enforcement
